note_claims.claim: The patient presents with left-sided sciatica-type leg pain for 3 weeks.
The onset of pain occurred 3 weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
Pain radiates from the buttock down the posterior thigh and lateral calf into the foot.
The leg pain is worse than the back pain.
Pain severity is up to 7/10.
Pain is worse after sitting for a while.
The patient experiences occasional tingling over the lateral foot.
The patient reports saddle numbness.
There is no change in bladder or bowel function.
The patient reports no fevers.
The patient has no history of cancer or unintentional weight loss.
The patient works as a care assistant.
The patient takes over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with little benefit.
The patient has no known drug allergies.
The patient has no history of peptic ulcer, asthma, or renal disease.
Lumbar flexion is limited by pain.
Straight leg raise is positive on the right at 40 degrees.
Straight leg raise is negative on the left.
Power, reflexes, and sensation are normal and symmetrical in both lower limbs.
The impression is right-sided sciatica, likely lumbar disc-related radiculopathy.
There are no red flags.
The plan is to stop ibuprofen.
The plan is to start naproxen 500 mg four times daily with food and omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 2 weeks.
The plan is to refer the patient to physiotherapy.
The patient is advised to keep active and avoid bed rest.
A fit note for 2 weeks is issued, allowing the patient to be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
The patient is scheduled for a review in 4 weeks.
The patient is advised to attend A&E immediately if they experience saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or bilateral leg weakness (cauda equina symptoms).
A symptom leaflet detailing these symptoms is given to the patient.

transcript_facts.fact: The patient reports having shooting pain going all the way down their leg.
The pain started about three weeks ago while lifting a resident at work.
The patient works as a care assistant at a nursing home.
The patient initially stated the pain was in the left leg, but corrected themselves to the right leg.
The pain radiates from the patient's bum, down the back of the thigh, round the outside of the calf, and into the foot.
The pain is rated seven out of ten on a bad day.
The pain is worse when the patient has been sitting for a while.
The patient experiences a bit of tingling on the outside of their foot sometimes.
The patient reports no weakness, only pain.
The patient denies numbness around their bottom or between their legs when sitting on the toilet.
The patient reports no change in their waterworks (trouble passing urine or leaking).
The patient reports no problems with their bowels or accidents.
The patient reports no fevers or feeling unwell.
The patient has no history of cancer or unintentional weight loss.
The patient has been taking Ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day, which they state 'barely touches it'.
The patient has no other medicines and no known drug allergies.
The patient reports no problems with their stomach, asthma, or kidneys.
The patient reports shooting pain when asked to bend forward, which shoots right down.
The pain is noted to be at about 40 degrees when the right leg is lifted straight.
The left leg is fine when lifted straight.
The patient's power, knee and ankle reflexes are normal in both legs.
The patient can feel touch on both sides of their body.
The clinician suggests the symptoms sound like sciatica, where a disc in the lower back is irritating a nerve going down the right leg.
The clinician states that most of these conditions settle over a few weeks to a couple of months.
The clinician plans to switch the patient from ibuprofen to naproxen 500 milligrams twice a day with food and add omeprazole 20 milligrams once a day for a couple of weeks.
The clinician plans to refer the patient to physiotherapy.
The clinician advises the patient to keep moving as much as possible rather than resting in bed.
The clinician plans to give the patient a fit note for two weeks, stating they may be fit for work with amended duties (no lifting or handling).
The clinician plans to see the patient again in four weeks.

The clinician provides safety-netting advice: if the patient experiences saddle numbness, difficulty passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, or weakness in both legs, they should go to A&E straight away.
The clinician gives the patient a leaflet with these symptoms.
